conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Lee, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My whole job is to support new mothers as they adjust to life with baby, and that includes checking in on how you’re feeling emotionally.

I’d like to spend the next few minutes with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us see whether common post-birth sadness or worry might have tipped into something we can ease together. Nothing you say will leave this room except in a summary note to your own OB/midwife, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you this past week.

We’ll keep it conversational: I’ll ask each question in everyday language, you tell me what feels closest to your experience, and we’ll move on. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—whether it’s a silly meme, a sitcom, or your partner’s goofy jokes?

Honestly…? I can’t remember the last time I laughed out loud. I’ll smile politely when my husband shows me something he thinks is hilarious, but it feels forced. Inside, it’s like there’s this heavy blanket smothering the humor. I used to laugh all the time—before the baby, I could giggle at the dumbest stuff—but this week, nothing feels funny. I guess that means “not at all” or “definitely not as much as I used to.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’m… not really. Nothing seems funny lately. I try to smile when my husband jokes around, but it feels fake. Mostly I just feel tired or numb.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—grabbing coffee with a friend, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like one more chore. I still do the things, but the “looking-forward” part isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s something I did—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not soothing him right. When he wouldn’t latch yesterday, I sat there crying, telling myself I’m already failing him. Even spilling a little pumped milk felt like I’d ruined everything. I know, rationally, it’s not all my fault, but the guilt just jumps in first.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart starts racing—like, what if she stops breathing the second I put her down? Or I’ll lie awake picturing her getting sick even though she’s perfectly fine. There’s no real reason, but the worry just barges in and parks itself there.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… sometimes it hits me out of nowhere. Like yesterday, I was just folding her onesies and suddenly my chest felt tight, heart pounding, like something awful was about to happen. I couldn’t tell you what—I just had to sit on the floor and breathe until it passed.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one thing—feeding, changing, pumping—there’s already another bottle to wash or diapers to prep, and the pile never shrinks. Some afternoons I just stare at the mess and feel like I’m drowning, but I still push through. I haven’t had anything to drink or take for it; I just keep going until I can finally close my eyes at night.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning—did I burp her long enough, is she still breathing, am I doing any of this right? Some nights I can’t fall asleep at all; other nights I jolt awake at 2 a.m. and can’t drift off again. It’s like the sadness and worry just keep replaying on a loop the second the lights go out.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… a lot of the time. I’ll be rocking the baby and tears just start leaking out, or I’ll catch myself staring out the window feeling this heavy emptiness. I wouldn’t say every single moment, but most days this week it’s been pretty constant.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes. I’ve cried several times this week—sometimes over little things, sometimes over nothing I can even name. I’ll just be sitting there and the tears start. It feels like the sadness just spills out whether I want it to or not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… never. I feel low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of my baby.

You've shared that the joy you once found in everyday moments feels distant now; instead, most days are clouded by heavy <sym>sadness</sym>, relentless <sym>worry</sym>, and a sense of drowning under ordinary tasks. You described forcing smiles when your husband jokes, lying awake haunted by "what-ifs," and blaming yourself whenever your baby fusses. Despite these struggles, you remain committed to caring for your infant and have not harbored any thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes total loss of ability to find things funny, forcing fake smiles and feeling numb, aligning with 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Response shows clear loss of anticipatory pleasure in daily activities, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, immediate self-blame for routine infant behaviors and minor mishaps, consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes daily, intrusive, irrational worries that intrude during routine tasks, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart) that arose without a clear trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm ('most days'), feeling 'drowning' amid unending tasks, yet still pushing through—best fits 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption driven by persistent unhappiness and worry, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "most of the time" and describes frequent crying and persistent emptiness this week.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent crying spells multiple times this week, often without clear triggers, indicating pervasive sadness consistent with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24/30 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Endorsements on items 1-9 map onto core <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>: most-days low mood, marked loss of interest/pleasure, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, concentration difficulty, and sleep disturbance, with onset within weeks postpartum. High scores on items 3, 4, 5 highlight prominent <sym>anxiety</sym>/<sym>panic</sym> features common in peripartum presentations. This pattern signals clinically significant distress requiring immediate evaluation and treatment planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>OB/midwife</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review these results and discuss treatment options
2. Ask for referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or psychiatry team familiar with breastfeeding-compatible medications
3. Begin evidence-based talk therapy such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>CBT</mod> focused on postpartum issues
4. Involve trusted family/friends in daily tasks and overnight shifts where possible to protect limited sleep
5. Practice brief self-care routines (10-minute shower, short outdoor walk, balanced snacks) even if motivation is low
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and intervention response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening Summary – Postpartum EPDS-equivalent (informal)

Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wks post-delivery, breastfeeding, no self-harm ideation endorsed.

Key endorsed items (frequency: “yes/often” unless noted)
- Anhedonia: marked loss of pleasure/interest (Q1, Q2)
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness most days (Q8, Q9)
- Sleep disturbance clearly linked to ruminating worry/sadness (Q7)
- Excessive guilt/self-blame re infant care (Q3)
- Daily free-floating anxiety, situational panic symptoms (Q4, Q5)
- Sense of being overwhelmed, “drowning” in tasks (Q6)
- Denies suicidal or self-harm thoughts (Q10)

Pattern: symptoms cluster consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with prominent anxiety; functional impact on sleep, self-care, and parenting confidence; no safety concerns at present.

Screening significance: high likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode; recommend formal EPDS, PHQ-9/GAD-7, and immediate referral to OB mental-health liaison or perinatal psychiatry for evaluation and treatment planning.
